'''''Memento''''' is a 2000<!-- THE FIRST RELEASE DATE IS THE RELEASE YEAR!!! --> American [[neo-noir]] [[psychological thriller film]] written for the screen and directed by [[Christopher Nolan]], based on the 2001 short story "[[Memento Mori (short story)|Memento Mori]]" by his brother, [[Jonathan Nolan]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.allmovie.com/movie/v220920|title=Memento (2000)|work=[[AllMovie]]|access-date=November 8, 2021|archive-date=January 22, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220122001206/https://www.allmovie.com/movie/v220920|url-status=live}}</ref> The film stars [[Guy Pearce]], [[Carrie-Anne Moss]], and [[Joe Pantoliano]]. It follows Leonard Shelby (Pearce), a man who has [[anterograde amnesia]]—resulting in the inability to form new long-term memories—and uses an elaborate system of photographs, handwritten notes, and tattoos sprawled across his body in an attempt to uncover the perpetrator who killed his wife and caused him to sustain the condition.

The film's [[non-linear narrative]] is presented as two different sequences of scenes interspersed during the film: a series in [[black-and-white]] that is shown chronologically, and a series of color sequences shown in [[reverse chronology|reverse order]] (simulating for the audience the mental state of the protagonist). The two sequences meet at the end of the film, producing one complete and cohesive narrative.<ref name=Klein>{{cite web | url = http://www.salon.com/2001/06/28/memento_analysis/ | title = Everything you wanted to know about "Memento" | work = [[Salon (website)|Salon]] | date = June 28, 2001 | access-date = September 4, 2012 | first = Andy | last = Klein | archive-date = June 15, 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200615172117/https://www.salon.com/2001/06/28/memento_analysis/ | url-status = live }}</ref>

''Memento'' premiered at the [[57th Venice International Film Festival|Venice Film Festival]] on September 5, 2000, and was theatrically released in the United States on March 16, 2001. It was acclaimed by critics, who praised its nonlinear structure and themes of memory, perception, grief, and self-deception. It was a commercial success, earning $40 million against a $9 million budget and gained a [[Cult film|cult following]]. ''Memento'' received many accolades, including the [[Waldo Salt Screenwriting Award]] at the [[Sundance Film Festival]], and [[Academy Award]] nominations for [[Best Original Screenplay]] and [[Academy Award for Best Film Editing|Best Film Editing]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=The 74th Academy Awards |url=https://www.oscars.org/oscars/ceremonies/2002 |access-date=May 5, 2023 |website=oscars.org |archive-date=October 1, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141001074138/https://www.oscars.org/awards/academyawards/legacy/ceremony/74th-winners.html |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2017, the United States [[Library of Congress]] deemed the film "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" and selected it for preservation in the [[National Film Registry]].

==Plot==
The film starts with a [[Instant film|Polaroid]] photograph of a dead man. As the sequence plays in reverse, the photo reverts to its undeveloped state, entering the camera before the man is shot in the head. The film continues, alternating between [[black-and-white]] and color sequences.

The black-and-white sequences begin with Leonard Shelby, a former [[insurance investigator]], in a motel room speaking to an unseen and unknown caller. Leonard has [[anterograde amnesia]] and is unable to store recent memories, the result of an attack by two men. Leonard explains that he killed the attacker who raped and strangled his wife Catherine, but a second clubbed him and escaped. The police did not accept that there was a second attacker, but Leonard believes the attacker's name is "John G" or "James G". Leonard investigates using notes, Polaroid photos, and tattoos to keep track of the information he discovers. Leonard recalls Sammy Jankis, another anterograde amnesiac, from his insurance industry days. After tests confirmed Sammy's inability to learn tasks through repetition, Leonard believed that his condition was at best psychological and turned down his insurance claim. Sammy's distraught wife repeatedly asked Sammy to administer her [[insulin]] shots for her [[diabetes]], hoping he would remember having recently given her a shot and avoid giving her a fatal overdose. However, Sammy administered each injection, and his wife died.

The color sequences are shown reverse-chronologically. In the story's chronology, Leonard self-directively gets a tattoo of John G's license plate. Finding a note in his clothes, he meets Natalie, a bartender who resents Leonard because he wears the clothes and drives the car of her boyfriend, Jimmy Grantz. After understanding Leonard's condition, she uses it to get Leonard to drive a man named Dodd out of town and offers to run the license plate as a favor through the Department of Motor Vehicle's database. Meanwhile, Leonard meets with a contact, Teddy, who helps with Dodd, but warns about Natalie. Leonard finds that he had previously annotated his Polaroid of Teddy, warning himself not to trust Teddy. Natalie provides Leonard with the driver's license for a John Edward Gammell, Teddy's full name. Confirming Leonard's information on "John G" and his warnings, Leonard drives Teddy to an abandoned building, leading to the opening where he shoots him.

In the final black-and-white sequence, prompted by the caller, Leonard meets with Teddy, an undercover officer, who has found Leonard's "John G", Jimmy, and directs Leonard to the abandoned building. When Jimmy arrives, Leonard strangles him fatally and takes a Polaroid photo of the body. As the photo develops, the black-and-white transitions to the final color sequence. Leonard swaps clothes with Jimmy, hearing him whisper "Sammy". As Leonard has only told Sammy's story to those he has met, he suddenly doubts Jimmy's role in his wife's murder. Teddy arrives and asserts that Jimmy was John G, but when Leonard is undeterred, Teddy reveals that he helped him kill the real attacker a year ago, and Teddy has been using Leonard since. Teddy points out that since the name "John G" is common, Leonard will cyclically forget and begin his search again and that even Teddy himself has a "John G" name. Further, Teddy reveals that Sammy's story is Leonard's own story, a memory Leonard has repressed to escape feelings of guilt.

After hearing Teddy confess all of this, Leonard burns the photograph of the dead Jimmy and the photo of himself right after killing the real attacker a year ago, pointing to his chest where he would get a tattoo to document his successful revenge. In a [[monologue]], Leonard explains that he is willing to lie to himself in order to get justice against anyone who has wronged him. He targets Teddy by ordering a tattoo of Teddy's license plate number and writing a note to himself that Teddy is not to be trusted so that he will mistake Teddy for John G and kill him. Leonard drives off in Jimmy's car, confident that, despite this lie, he will retain enough awareness of the world to know that his actions have consequences.

==Film structure==
[[File:Memento Timeline.png|thumb|A diagram depicting the structure of ''Memento'']]

The film is structured with two [[timeline]]s: color sequences are alternated with black-and-white sequences. The latter are put together in chronological order. The color ones are [[reverse chronology|ordered in reverse]]. Chronologically, the black-and-white sequences come first, the color sequences come next.

Using the numbering scheme suggested by Andy Klein—who took numbers from 1 to 22 for the black-and-white sequences and letters A–V for the color ones in his article for [[Salon magazine|''Salon'']] magazine<ref name=Klein/>—the plotting of the film as presented is: Opening credits (shown in reverse), 1, V, 2, U, 3, T, 4, S, ..., 22/A, credits.

There is a smooth transition from the black-and-white sequence 22 to color sequence A, which occurs during the development of a Polaroid photograph.

The chronological order of the story can be viewed as a "hidden feature" on the 2-Disc Limited Edition [[DVD region code#1|Region 1]] [[DVD]]<ref>{{cite web |last=Holm |first=D.K. |title=2-Disc LE DVD Review |url=http://www.dvdjournal.com/reviews/m/memento_le.shtml |access-date=September 24, 2009 |website=DVD Journal |archive-date=October 26, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211026092505/http://www.dvdjournal.com/reviews/m/memento_le.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref> and the 3-Disc special Edition [[DVD region code#2|Region 2]] DVD.<ref>{{cite web |last=Papamichael |first=Stella |title=3 Disk SE DVD Review |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/films/2004/12/15/memento_se_2004_dvd_review.shtml |access-date=September 24, 2009 |website=BBC |archive-date=May 13, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220513061648/https://www.bbc.co.uk/films/2004/12/15/memento_se_2004_dvd_review.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref> In this special feature, the chapters of the film are put together into the chronological order and is shown: Ending Credits (run in reverse), 1, 2, 3, ..., 22/A, B, ..., V, then the opening title runs "backward" to what was shown (the opening title sequence is run in reverse during the actual film, so it is shown forward in this version).

Stefano Ghislotti wrote an article in ''Film Anthology''<ref>{{cite web|url=http://dinamico2.unibg.it/fa/fa_mem01.html |title=Backwards: Memory and Fabula Construction in "Memento" by Christopher Nolan |work=Film Anthology |year=2003 |access-date=September 24, 2009 |first=Stefano |last=Ghislotti |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091231020648/http://dinamico2.unibg.it/fa/fa_mem01.html |archive-date=December 31, 2009}}</ref> which discusses how Nolan provides the viewer with the clues necessary to decode the plot as we watch and help us understand the chronology. The color sequences include a brief overlap to help clue the audience into the fact that they are being presented in reverse order. The purpose of the fragmented reverse sequencing is to force the audience into a sympathetic experience of Leonard's defective ability to create new long-term memories, where prior events are not recalled, since the audience has yet to see them.

==Production==

===Development===
In July 1996, brothers [[Christopher Nolan|Christopher]] and [[Jonathan Nolan]] took a cross-country road trip from [[Chicago]] to [[Los Angeles]], as Christopher was relocating to the American West Coast. During the drive, Jonathan [[Pitch (filmmaking)|pitched]] the story for the film to his brother, who responded enthusiastically to the idea.<ref>{{cite news | last=Kaufman | first=Anthony | title=Mindgames; Christopher Nolan Remembers "Memento" | website=IndieWire.com | url=https://www.indiewire.com/article/decade_christopher_nolan_on_memento/ | date=December 4, 2009 | access-date=August 20, 2010 | archive-date=March 24, 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160324053252/http://www.indiewire.com/article/decade_christopher_nolan_on_memento | url-status=live }}</ref> After they arrived in Los Angeles, Jonathan left for Washington, D.C. to finish college at [[Georgetown University]]. The mysterious killer character known only as "John G." was actually an homage to Jonathan's Georgetown University screenwriting professor at the time, John Glavin.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/meet-the-tough-professor-who-inspired-jonathan-nolan-and-john-mulaney/2017/11/30/5f94d35c-be52-11e7-959c-fe2b598d8c00_story.html|title=Meet the tough professor who inspired Jonathan Nolan and John Mulaney|newspaper=Washington Post|language=en|access-date=2019-04-16|archive-date=April 16, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190416072323/https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/meet-the-tough-professor-who-inspired-jonathan-nolan-and-john-mulaney/2017/11/30/5f94d35c-be52-11e7-959c-fe2b598d8c00_story.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Christopher repeatedly asked Jonathan to send him a first draft, and after a few months, Jonathan complied.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=[https://archive.org/details/makingofmemento00mott/page/162 162]}} Two months later, Christopher came up with the idea to tell the film backwards, and began to work on the screenplay. Jonathan wrote the short story simultaneously, and the brothers continued to correspond, sending each other subsequent revisions of their respective works.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=166}} Christopher initially wrote the script as a linear story, and then would "go back and reorder it the way it is on screen to check the logic of it."<ref>{{cite news|last=Neff|first=Renfreu|title=Remembering Where it All Began: Christopher Nolan on Memento|url=http://creativescreenwriting.com/remembering-where-it-all-began-christopher-nolan-on-memento/|access-date=July 27, 2015|newspaper=CreativeScreenwriting.com|date=July 20, 2015|archive-date=July 27, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150727010748/http://creativescreenwriting.com/remembering-where-it-all-began-christopher-nolan-on-memento/|url-status=live}}</ref> Nolan was also influenced by the short story "[[Funes the Memorious]]" by [[Jorge Luis Borges]]. "I think ''Memento'' is a strange cousin to 'Funes the Memorious'—about a man who remembers everything, who can't forget anything. It's a bit of an inversion of that."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nolanfans.com/forums/viewtopic.php?f=10&t=4914|title="Memento" Q&A with Chris Nolan and Guillermo del Toro {{!}} Nolan Fans Forums|website=www.nolanfans.com|access-date=2019-03-16|archive-date=June 15, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200615135635/https://www.nolanfans.com/forums/viewtopic.php?f=10&t=4914|url-status=live}}</ref>

Jonathan's short story, titled "[[Memento Mori (short story)|Memento Mori]]", is radically different from Christopher's film, although it maintains the same essential elements. In Jonathan's version, Leonard is instead named Earl and is a patient at a [[mental institution]].{{sfn|Mottram|2002|pp=183–95}}<ref name=SS>{{cite web|url=http://www.impulsenine.com/homepage/pages/shortstories/memento_mori.htm |title=Memento Mori |work=[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]] |year=2001 |access-date=October 2, 2010 |first=Jonathan |last=Nolan |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100922083236/http://www.impulsenine.com/homepage/pages/shortstories/memento_mori.htm |archive-date=September 22, 2010}}</ref> As in the film, his wife was killed by an anonymous man, and during the attack on his wife, Earl lost his ability to create new long-term memories. Like Leonard, Earl leaves notes to himself and has tattoos with information about the killer. However, in the short story, Earl convinces himself through his own written notes to escape the mental institution and murder his wife's killer. Unlike the film, there is no ambiguity that Earl finds and kills the anonymous man.<ref name=SS/>

In July 1997, Christopher Nolan's girlfriend (later wife) [[Emma Thomas]] showed his screenplay to [[Aaron Ryder]], an executive for [[Newmarket Films]]. Ryder said the script was, "perhaps the most innovative script I had ever seen",{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=176}} and soon after, it was optioned by Newmarket and given a budget of $4.5&nbsp;million.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=177}} Pre-production lasted seven weeks, during which the main shooting location changed from [[Montreal]], Quebec to [[Los Angeles]], California, to create a more realistic and ''[[film noir|noirish]]'' atmosphere for the film.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=151-152}}

===Casting===
[[Brad Pitt]] was initially slated to play Leonard. Pitt was interested in the part, but passed due to scheduling conflicts.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=106}}<ref>{{cite web | url=https://uk.movies.yahoo.com/christopher-nolan-reveals-the-truth-behind-the-brad-pitt-memento-rumours-153202005.html | title=Christopher Nolan reveals the truth behind the Brad Pitt Memento rumours | date=January 19, 2014 | access-date=October 2, 2023 | archive-date=July 2, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230702054034/https://uk.movies.yahoo.com/christopher-nolan-reveals-the-truth-behind-the-brad-pitt-memento-rumours-153202005.html | url-status=live }}</ref> Other considered actors included [[Charlie Sheen]], [[Alec Baldwin]], [[Aaron Eckhart]] (who later worked with Nolan on ''[[The Dark Knight]]''), and [[Thomas Jane]], but the role went to [[Guy Pearce]], who impressed Nolan the most. Pearce was chosen partly for his "lack of celebrity" (after Pitt passed, they "decided to eschew the pursuit of [[A-list]] stars and make the film for less money by using an affordable quality actor") and his enthusiasm for the role, evidenced by a personal phone call Pearce made to Nolan to discuss the part.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|pp=107-108}}<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.empireonline.com/movies/features/memento-guy-pearce-interview-working-with-christopher-nolan/ | title=Memento: Guy Pearce on Why Working with Christopher Nolan Was One of His Greatest Life Experiences | date=August 17, 2020 }}</ref>

After being impressed by [[Carrie-Anne Moss]]'s performance as [[Trinity (The Matrix)|Trinity]] in the 1999 [[science fiction]] film ''[[The Matrix]]'', Jennifer Todd suggested her for the part of Natalie. While [[Mary McCormack]] lobbied for the role, Nolan decided to cast Moss as Natalie, saying, "She added an enormous amount to the role of Natalie that wasn't on the page".{{Sfn|Mottram|2002|p=111}} For the corrupt police officer Teddy, "comedian [[Denis Leary]] was mentioned, though proved unavailable".{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=112}} Moss suggested her co-star from ''The Matrix'', [[Joe Pantoliano]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Interview with Joe Pantoliano (Part 2 of 2)|date=April 4, 2001|website=[[IGN]]|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2001/04/04/interview-with-joe-pantoliano-part-2-of-2|access-date=February 6, 2017|archive-date=May 13, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220513061648/https://www.ign.com/articles/2001/04/04/interview-with-joe-pantoliano-part-2-of-2|url-status=live}}</ref> Although there was a concern that Pantoliano might be too villainous for the part, he was still cast and Nolan said he was surprised by the actor's subtlety in his performance.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=112}}

The rest of the film's characters were quickly cast after the three main leads were established. [[Stephen Tobolowsky]] and [[Harriet Sansom Harris]] play Sammy Jankis and his wife, respectively. [[Mark Boone Junior]] landed the role of Burt, the motel clerk, because Jennifer Todd liked his "look and attitude" for the part (as a result he has re-appeared in minor roles in other productions by Nolan).{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=114}} Tobolowsky said that he took the role of Sammy Jankis as he liked the script and also he knew the role was perfect for him as he had suffered from amnesia in real life.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.denofgeek.com/movies/memento-sammy-jankis-stephen-tobolowsky/ | title=Memento and the Significance of Sammy Jankis | website=Den of Geek | date=March 16, 2021 | access-date=April 1, 2023 | archive-date=April 1, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401111710/https://www.denofgeek.com/movies/memento-sammy-jankis-stephen-tobolowsky/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

===Filming===
Filming took place from September 7 to October 8, 1999,{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=125}} a 25-day shooting schedule. Pearce was on set every day during filming, although all three principal actors (including Pantoliano and Moss) performed together only on the first day, shooting exterior sequences outside Natalie's house. All of Moss' scenes were completed in the first week,{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=127}} including follow-up scenes at Natalie's home, Ferdy's bar, and the restaurant where she meets Leonard for the final time.

Pantoliano returned to the set late in the second week to continue filming his scenes. On September 25, the crew shot the opening scene in which Leonard kills Teddy. Although the scene is in reverse motion, Nolan used forward-played sounds.<ref name=dvdcom>{{cite video | people=Nolan, Christopher | title=Memento DVD commentary | medium=DVD | publisher=Columbia TriStar |date=2002 }}</ref> For a shot of a shell casing flying upwards, the shell had to be dropped in front of the camera in forward motion, but it constantly rolled out of frame. Nolan was forced to blow the casing out of frame instead, but in the confusion, the crew shot it backwards.<ref name=dvdcom/> They then had to make an optical (a copy of the shot) and reverse the shot to make it go forward again. "That was the height of complexity in terms of the film", Nolan said. "An optical to make a backwards running shot forwards, and the forwards shot is a simulation of a backwards shot."{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=133}}

The next day, on September 26, Larry Holden returned to shoot the sequence where Leonard attacks Jimmy.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=134}} After filming was completed five days later, Pearce's [[voice-over]]s were recorded. For the black-and-white scenes, Pearce was given free rein to improvise his narrative, allowing for a documentary feel.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=133}}

The Travel Inn in [[Sunland-Tujunga, Los Angeles|Tujunga, California]], was repainted and used as the interior of Leonard's and Dodd's motel rooms and the exterior of the film's Discount Inn. Scenes in Sammy Jankis' house were shot in a suburban home close to [[Pasadena, California|Pasadena]], while Natalie's house was located in [[Burbank, California|Burbank]].{{sfn|Mottram|2002|pp=154-155}} The crew planned to shoot the derelict building set (where Leonard kills Teddy and Jimmy) in a Spanish-styled brick building owned by a train company. However, one week before shooting began, the company placed several dozen train carriages outside the building, making the exterior unfilmable. Since the interior of the building had already been built as a set, a new location had to be found. An oil refinery near [[Long Beach, California|Long Beach]] was used instead, and the scene where Leonard burns his wife's possessions was filmed on the other side of the refinery.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|pp=156-157}}

===Music===
[[David Julyan]] composed the film's [[Synthesizer|synthesized]] score. Julyan acknowledges several synthesized soundtracks that inspired him, such as [[Vangelis]]'s ''[[Blade Runner (soundtrack)|Blade Runner]]'' and [[Hans Zimmer]]'s ''[[The Thin Red Line (soundtrack)|The Thin Red Line]]''.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=92, 96}} While composing the score, Julyan created different, distinct sounds to differentiate between the color and black-and-white scenes: "brooding and classical" themes in the former, and "oppressive and rumbly noise" in the latter.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=96}} Since he describes the entire score as "Leonard's theme", Julyan says, "The emotion I was aiming at with my music was yearning and loss. But a sense of loss you feel but at the same time you don't know what it is you have lost, a sense of being adrift."<ref>{{cite web | last=Julyan | first=David | title=Comments on Memento | website=Davidjulyan.com |url=http://www.davidjulyan.com/scores.html| access-date=August 8, 2007 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070717155838/http://www.davidjulyan.com/scores.html |archive-date = July 17, 2007}}</ref>

Initially, Nolan wanted to use [[Radiohead]]'s "[[Paranoid Android]]" during the end credits, but he was unable to secure the rights.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=99}} Instead, [[David Bowie]]'s "[[Something in the Air (David Bowie song)|Something in the Air]]" is used, although another of Radiohead's songs, an extended version of "[[Treefingers]]", is included on the film's soundtrack.<ref>{{cite web | title=Track Listing for "Memento: Music For and Inspired by the Film" | website=CDuniverse.com | url=http://www.cduniverse.com/search/xx/music/pid/1824606/a/Memento.htm | access-date=August 8, 2007 | archive-date=October 20, 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121020130700/http://www.cduniverse.com/search/xx/music/pid/1824606/a/Memento.htm | url-status=live }}</ref>

==Release==
The film gained substantial [[word-of-mouth]] press from the [[film festival]] circuit. It premiered at the [[57th Venice International Film Festival|2000]] [[Venice Film Festival]], where it received a standing ovation, and afterwards played at [[Deauville American Film Festival]] and the [[Toronto International Film Festival]].{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=62-64}} With the publicity from these events, ''Memento'' did not have trouble finding foreign distributors, opening in more than 20 countries worldwide. Its promotion tour ended at the [[Sundance Film Festival]], where it played in January 2001.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=65}}

Finding American distributors proved more troublesome. ''Memento'' was screened for various studio heads (including [[Miramax]] chief [[Harvey Weinstein]]) in March 2000. Although most of the executives loved the film and praised Nolan's talent, all passed on distributing the picture, believing it was too confusing and would not attract a large audience.<ref name=EW>{{cite web | last=Fierman | first=Daniel | title=Memory Swerves: EW reports on the story behind the indie thriller | magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] | url=https://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,103696,00.html | date=March 21, 2001 | url-status=dead | access-date=August 9, 2007 | archive-date=February 22, 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222003957/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,103696,00.html }}</ref> After famed [[independent film]] director [[Steven Soderbergh]] saw the film and learned it was not being distributed, he championed the film in interviews and public events,{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=52}} giving it even more publicity, although he did not secure a distributor. Newmarket, in a financially risky move, decided to distribute the film itself.<ref name=EW/>

After the first few weeks of distribution, ''Memento'' had reached more than 500 theaters and earned a domestic total of $25&nbsp;million in its box-office run. The film's success was surprising to those who passed on the film, so much so that Weinstein realized his mistake and tried to buy the film from Newmarket.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=58}}

===Marketing===
Jonathan Nolan designed the film's official website. As with the marketing strategy of ''[[The Blair Witch Project]]'', the website was intended to provide further clues and hints to introduce the story, while not providing any concrete information.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=67}} After a short intro on the website, the viewer is shown a newspaper clipping detailing Leonard's murder of Teddy. Clicking on highlighted words in the article leads to more material describing the film, including Leonard's notes and photographs as well as police reports.<ref>{{cite web | title=Official site | website=otnemem.com | url=http://www.otnemem.com | access-date=August 9, 2007 | archive-date=March 4, 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200304024059/http://www.otnemem.com/ | url-status=live }}</ref> The filmmakers employed another tactic by sending out Polaroid pictures to random people, depicting a bloody and shirtless Leonard pointing at an unmarked spot on his chest.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=74}} Since Newmarket distributed the film, Christopher Nolan edited the film's trailers.{{sfn|Mottram|2002|p=74}} Sold to inexpensive [[cable channel]]s like [[Bravo (US TV channel)|Bravo]] and [[A&E Network|A&E]], and websites such as [[Yahoo]] and [[MSN]], the trailers were key to the film gaining widespread public notice.

===Home media===
[[File:Mementomenupic.JPG|thumb|270px|The Special Edition DVD's menus are arranged as items in a [[psychological test]]. Highlighting certain objects leads to special features.]]
''Memento'' was released on [[DVD]] and [[VHS]] in the United States and Canada on September 4, 2001, and in the United Kingdom on January 14, 2002. The UK edition contains a hidden feature that allows the viewer to watch the film in chronological order. The Canadian version does not have this feature but the film chapters are set up to do this manually or through DVD programming. The original US release does not have the chronological feature nor are the chapters set up correctly to do it.

The film was re-released in a limited edition DVD that features an audio commentary by Christopher Nolan, with four different endings; the original short story by Jonathan Nolan on which the film was based; and an episode of the [[Sundance Channel (United States)|Sundance Channel]] series ''[[Anatomy of a Scene]]'' documenting the making of the film.<ref name="DVD" /> The limited edition DVD also contains a hidden feature that allows the viewer to watch the film in chronological order.<ref name="DVD">{{cite news| last=Bovberg| first=Jason| title=Memento: Limited Edition| website=DVDtalk.com| url=https://www.dvdtalk.com/reviews/3815/memento-limited-edition/| date=May 4, 2002| access-date=March 6, 2022| archive-date=November 28, 2022| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221128010954/https://www.dvdtalk.com/reviews/3815/memento-limited-edition/| url-status=live}}</ref>

The Limited Edition DVD is packaged to look like Leonard's case file from a mental institution, with notes scribbled by "doctors" and Leonard on the inside.<ref name="DVD"/> The DVD menus are designed as a series of [[psychological tests]]; the viewer has to choose certain words, objects, and multiple choice answers to play the movie or access special features.<ref name="DVD"/> Leonard's "notes" on the DVD case offer clues to navigating the DVD. Some of the "materials" seem designed to induce paranoia and uncertainty (a picture of one person whispering to another is captioned, "They know what you did"), alluding to Shelby's mental state.

''Memento'' was re-released in the UK on a 3-disc Special Edition DVD on December 27, 2004. This release contains all the special features that are on the two US releases in one package plus a couple of new interviews. The menus appear as tattoos on Leonard's body and are more straightforward than the US 2-disc limited edition DVD.

''Memento'' was released on [[Blu-ray]] on August 15, 2006. This release lacks the special features contained on the Limited Edition DVD, but does include the audio commentary by director Christopher Nolan. The single-layer disc features an [[MPEG]]-2 [[1080p]] transfer and [[Pulse-code modulation|PCM]] 5.1 surround audio. The film was also released on [[iTunes]] as a [[Digital distribution|digital download]].

The film was re-released on the Blu-ray and DVD in the US on February 22, 2011, by Lionsgate following the 10th anniversary of the film. Both the Blu-ray and DVD have a new transfer that was also shown in theaters. Aside from the transfer, the Blu-ray contains a new special featurette by Nolan on the film's legacy.<ref name="10th Anniv. Ed.">{{cite web |url=http://www.blu-ray.com/news/?id=5561 |title=The Last Unicorn, Memento 10th Anniversary Blu-ray Announced |last=Calonge |first=Juan |date=December 2, 2010 |website=Blu-ray.com |access-date=December 2, 2010 |archive-date=May 13, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220513061648/https://www.blu-ray.com/news/?id=5561 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Reception==

===Box office===
''Memento'' was a box office success. In the United States, during its opening weekend, it was released in only 11 theaters, but by week 11 it was distributed to more than 500 theaters.<ref name=weekend>{{cite web | title=Memento Weekend Box Office | website=[[Box Office Mojo]] | url=https://boxofficemojo.com/movies/?page=weekend&id=memento.htm | access-date=December 18, 2006 | archive-date=December 8, 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181208133046/https://www.boxofficemojo.com/movies/?page=weekend&id=memento.htm | url-status=live }}</ref> It grossed over $25&nbsp;million in North America and $14&nbsp;million in other countries, combining for a total worldwide gross of $40&nbsp;million.<ref name=num/><ref name="Mojo" /> During its theatrical run, it did not place higher than eighth in the list of highest-grossing movies for a single weekend.<ref name="weekend" />

=== Critical response ===
''Memento'' was met with critical acclaim. On review aggregator [[Rotten Tomatoes]], the film received an approval rating of 93% based on 184 reviews, with an average rating of 8.8/10. The site's critical consensus reads, "Christopher Nolan skillfully guides the audience through ''Memento''{{'s}} fractured narrative, seeping his film in existential dread."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/memento/ |title=Memento (2000) |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=[[Fandango Media|Fandango]] |access-date=May 30, 2025|archive-date=November 27, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221127105534/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/memento |url-status=live }}</ref> On [[Metacritic]], the film has a weighted average score of 83 out of 100 based on 34 critics, indicating "universal acclaim".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.metacritic.com/movie/memento |title=Memento Reviews |website=[[Metacritic]] |publisher=[[CBS Interactive]] |access-date=July 31, 2018 |archive-date=December 28, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171228202623/http://www.metacritic.com/movie/memento |url-status=live }}</ref>

Film critic [[James Berardinelli]] gave the film four out of four stars, ranking it number one on his year-end Top Ten list and number sixty-three on his All-Time Top 100 films.<ref>{{cite news |last=Berardinelli |first=James |author-link=James Berardinelli |date=December 31, 2001 |title=Berardinelli's Top Ten for 2001 |website=ReelViews.net |url=http://preview.reelviews.net/comment/123101.html |url-status=dead |access-date=December 16, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221231155805/https://preview.reelviews.net/comment/123101.html |archive-date=2022-12-31}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Berardinelli |first=James |title=Berardinelli's All-Time Top 100 |website=ReelViews.net |url=http://preview.reelviews.net/top100/toc.html |url-status=dead |access-date=December 16, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150420111431/http://preview.reelviews.net/top100/toc.html |archive-date=April 20, 2015}}</ref> In his review, he called it an "endlessly fascinating, wonderfully open-ended motion picture [that] will be remembered by many who see it as one of the best films of the year".<ref name="Reelviews">{{cite news |last=Berardinelli |first=James |title=Memento |website=ReelViews.net |url=http://preview.reelviews.net/movies/m/memento.html |url-status=dead |access-date=December 16, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191114182740/http://preview.reelviews.net/movies/m/memento.html |archive-date=November 14, 2019}}</ref> Berardinelli praised the film's backwards narrative, saying that "what really distinguishes this film is its brilliant, innovative structure", and noted that Guy Pearce gives an "astounding ... tight, and thoroughly convincing performance".<ref name="Reelviews"/> In 2009, Berardinelli chose ''Memento'' as his #3 best movie of the decade. William Arnold of the ''[[Seattle Post-Intelligencer]]'' writes that ''Memento'' is a "delicious one-time treat", and emphasizes that director Christopher Nolan "not only makes ''Memento'' work as a non-linear puzzle film, but as a tense, atmospheric thriller".<ref>{{cite news|last=Arnold | first=William |work=[[Seattle Post-Intelligencer]] |title=Memento is new, original, possibly even great |url=http://seattlep-i.nwsource.com/movies/mementoq.shtml |date=March 30, 2001 |access-date=December 16, 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080725052600/http://seattlep-i.nwsource.com/movies/mementoq.shtml |archive-date=July 25, 2008}}</ref> Rob Blackwelder noted that "Nolan has a crackerjack command over the intricacies of this story. He makes every single element of the film a clue to the larger picture ... as the story edges back toward the origins of [Leonard's] quest".<ref>{{cite news | last=Blackwelder | first=Rob | title=Blanks for the Memories | website=SPLICEDwire.com | url=http://splicedwire.com/01reviews/memento.html | access-date=December 18, 2006 | archive-date=December 11, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171211170253/http://splicedwire.com/01reviews/memento.html | url-status=live }}</ref>

Not all critics were impressed with the film's structure. Marjorie Baumgarten wrote, "In forward progression, the narrative would garner little interest, thus making the reverse storytelling a filmmaker's conceit."<ref>{{cite news | last=Baumgarten | first=Marjorie | title=Memento | work=[[Austin Chronicle]] | url=http://www.austinchronicle.com/gbase/Calendar/Film?Film=oid%3a141059 | date=March 30, 2001 | access-date=December 18, 2006 | archive-date=August 2, 2003 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030802052954/http://www.austinchronicle.com/gbase/Calendar/Film?Film=oid:141059 | url-status=live }}</ref> Sean Burns of the ''[[Philadelphia Weekly]]'' commented that "For all its formal wizardry, ''Memento'' is ultimately an ice-cold feat of intellectual gamesmanship. Once the visceral thrill of the puzzle structure begins to wear off, there's nothing left to hang onto. The film itself fades like one of Leonard's temporary memories."<ref>{{cite news |last=Burns | first=Sean | title=Ain't It the Truth? | work=[[Philadelphia Weekly]] | url=http://www.philadelphiaweekly.com/view.php?id=3751| date=March 28, 2001| access-date=December 18, 2006 |archive-url = https://archive.today/20041105000416/http://philadelphiaweekly.com/view.php?id=3751 |archive-date = November 5, 2004}}</ref> While [[Roger Ebert]] gave the film a favorable three out of four stars, he did not think it warranted multiple viewings. After watching ''Memento'' twice, he concluded that "Greater understanding helped on the plot level, but didn't enrich the viewing experience. Confusion is the state we are intended to be in."<ref>{{cite news |last=Ebert |first=Roger |author-link=Roger Ebert |date=April 13, 2001 |title=Memento |work=[[Chicago Sun-Times]] |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/memento-2001 |url-status=live |access-date=December 18, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121003112235/http://rogerebert.suntimes.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F20010413%2FREVIEWS%2F104130303%2F1023 |archive-date=October 3, 2012}}</ref> [[Jonathan Rosenbaum]] disliked the film, and commented in his review of ''[[Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind]]'' that ''Memento'' is a "gimmicky and unpoetic counterfeit" of [[Alain Resnais]]'s 1968 film ''[[Je t'aime, je t'aime]]''.<ref>{{cite news |last=Rosenbaum |first=Jonathan |author-link=Jonathan Rosenbaum |date=March 19, 2004 |title=A Stylist Hits His Stride |url=http://www.jonathanrosenbaum.net/?p=6070 |url-status=live |access-date=October 8, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210110143450/http://www.jonathanrosenbaum.net/2020/08/a-stylist-hits-his-stride/ |archive-date=January 10, 2021}}</ref>

In 2005, the [[Writers Guild of America]] ranked the [[screenplay]] #100 on its list of 101 Greatest Screenplays ever written.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wga.org/subpage_newsevents.aspx?id=1807 |last=Savage | first=Sophia |date=February 27, 2013 |title=WGA Lists Greatest Screenplays, From 'Casablanca' and 'Godfather' to 'Memento' and 'Notorious' |website=wga.org |access-date=February 28, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060813151310/http://www.wga.org/subpage_newsevents.aspx?id=1807 |archive-date=August 13, 2006}}</ref> In 2012, the [[Motion Picture Editors Guild]] listed the film as the fourteenth best-edited film of all time based on a survey of its membership.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal |date=May 2012 |title=The 75 Best Edited Films |url=https://cinemontage.org/75-best-edited-films/ |url-status=live |journal=Editors Guild Magazine |volume=1 |issue=3 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150317101140/https://www.editorsguild.com/magazine.cfm?ArticleID=1102 |archive-date=March 17, 2015}}</ref> ''Memento'' was considered "culturally, historically or aesthetically significant" by the US [[Library of Congress]] and was selected for preservation in the [[National Film Registry]] in 2017, the first narrative feature of the 2000s to be honored.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://variety.com/2017/film/news/the-goonies-titanic-field-of-dreams-die-hard-national-film-registry-1202638298/ |title='Titanic,' 'The Goonies,' 'Field of Dreams,' 'Memento' Added to National Film Registry |work=Variety |date=December 13, 2017 |access-date=December 13, 2017 |archive-date=December 13, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171213101146/http://variety.com/2017/film/news/the-goonies-titanic-field-of-dreams-die-hard-national-film-registry-1202638298/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2021, members of [[Writers Guild of America West]] (WGAW) and [[Writers Guild of America, East]] (WGAE) ranked its screenplay 10th in WGA’s 101 Greatest Screenplays of the 21st Century (so far).<ref>{{Cite web |title=101 Greatest Screenplays of the 21st Century (*so far) |url=https://www.wga.org/writers-room/101-best-lists/101-best-screenplays-of-the-21st-century-so-far/list |access-date=2025-12-26 |website=www.wga.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Pedersen |first=Erik |date=2021-12-06 |title=101 Greatest Screenplays Of The 21st Century: Horror Pic Tops Writers Guild's List |url=https://deadline.com/2021/12/greatest-screenplays-of-21st-century-list-writers-guild-get-out-1234885622/ |access-date=2025-12-26 |website=Deadline |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Scientific response===
Many medical experts have cited ''Memento'' as featuring one of the most realistic and accurate depictions of [[anterograde amnesia]]. [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]] neuroscientist [[Christof Koch]] called ''Memento'' "the most accurate portrayal of the different memory systems in the popular media",<ref>{{cite book| last=Koch| first=Christof| author-link=Christof Koch| title=The Quest for Consciousness: A Neurobiological Approach| publisher=Roberts and Company Publishers| year=2004| isbn=0-9747077-0-8| page=196}}</ref> while physician Esther M. Sternberg, Director of the Integrative Neural Immune Program at the [[National Institute of Mental Health]], identified the film as "close to a perfect exploration of the neurobiology of memory."<ref>{{cite journal| last=Sternberg| first=E.M| title=Piecing Together a Puzzling World: Memento| journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]]| volume=292| issue=5522| pages=1661–1662| date=June 1, 2001| doi=10.1126/science.1062103| s2cid=191345264}}</ref>

Sternberg concludes: {{blockquote|This thought-provoking thriller is the kind of movie that keeps reverberating in the viewer's mind, and each iteration makes one examine preconceived notions in a different light. ''Memento'' is a movie for anyone interested in the workings of memory and, indeed, in what it is that makes our own reality.}}

Clinical [[neuropsychology|neuropsychologist]] Sallie Baxendale writes in ''[[The BMJ]]'':

{{blockquote|The overwhelming majority of amnesic characters in films bear little relation to any [[neurology|neurological]] or [[psychiatry|psychiatric]] realities of memory loss. Apparently inspired partly by the neuropsychological studies of the famous patient [[HM (patient)|HM]] (who developed severe anterograde memory impairment after [[neurosurgery]] to control his [[epilepsy|epileptic]] seizures) and the [[temporal lobe]] amnesic syndrome, the film documents the difficulties faced by Leonard, who develops a severe anterograde amnesia after an attack in which his wife is killed. Unlike in most films in this genre, this amnesic character retains his identity, has little retrograde amnesia, and shows several of the severe everyday memory difficulties associated with the disorder. The fragmented, almost mosaic quality to the sequence of scenes in the film also reflects the 'perpetual present' nature of the syndrome.<ref>{{cite journal| last=Baxendale| first=Sallie| title=Memories aren't made of this: amnesia at the movies| journal=[[BMJ]]| volume=329| issue=7480| pages=1480–1483| date=December 18, 2004| doi=10.1136/bmj.329.7480.1480| pmid=15604191| pmc=535990}}</ref>}}

===Interpretations and analysis===
{{Main|Cinematic style of Christopher Nolan}}

{{quote box|width=30em|align=right|quote=By going backward in time, Memento draws the real mystery from viewers learning the first step in Leonard's investigation, the origins of his self-deception. Yes, we also learn what really happened to his wife, what happened to him, and what happened to his killer, and we understand more about Teddy's complicated role in using Leonard for his own purposes. But the most telling revelation, at the end of Memento, isn't limited to his condition: Leonard lies to himself. And when he isn't outright lying to himself, he's guilty of confirmation bias, accepting only the facts that affirm his pre-cooked conclusions, and tossing out all the rest.|salign=right|source=Scott Tobias, from ''The A.V. Club''<ref>{{cite web | last=Tobias | first=Scott | title=Memento's puzzle structure hides big twists and bigger profundities | url=https://www.avclub.com/article/imementois-puzzle-structure-hides-big-twists-and-b-88452 | work=[[The A.V. Club]] | date=November 8, 2012 | access-date=December 9, 2016 | archive-date=August 18, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170818232940/http://www.avclub.com/article/imementois-puzzle-structure-hides-big-twists-and-b-88452 | url-status=live }}</ref>}}

Since its release, ''Memento'' has been a widely noted topic of film discussion, both for its unique narrative structure and themes. Those searching for explanations of the film's plot have either resorted to online forums, message boards or scholarly material, or have ignored the film's official website and forums to maintain their own personal hypotheses.<ref>{{cite book | last=Molloy | first=Claire | date=2010 | title=American Indies: Memento | publisher=Edinburgh University Press | page=98 | isbn=9780748637713 }}</ref> On the same topic of self-deception, James Mooney of filmandphilosophy.com notes that the film suggests how "our memories deceive us, or rather, sometimes we deceive ourselves by 'choosing' to forget or by manipulating our memories of past events."<ref>{{cite web | last=Mooney | first=James | title=Memento: Memory and Identity | url=http://filmandphilosophy.com/2011/09/15/memento-mind-memory-and-personal-identity/ | work=Filmosophy | date=September 15, 2011 | access-date=December 9, 2016 | archive-date=June 25, 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210625042039/https://filmandphilosophy.com/2011/09/15/memento-mind-memory-and-personal-identity/ | url-status=dead }}</ref> This is much in line with a psychological analysis of the film, specifically the act of [[confabulation]]. Leonard's use of confabulation poses the dilemma, as explained by [[SUNY Downstate Medical Center]] Professor John Kubie for [[Society for Neuroscience|BrainFacts.org]]: "In ''Memento'' we are faced with the question of how much of Leonard's memory of the past is real and how much constructed from beliefs and wishes."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://blog.brainfacts.org/2013/08/memento-and-personal-identity/#.VX8Bf_lVhBc|title=Memento and Personal Identity|last=Kubie|first=John|website=blog.brainfacts.org|publisher=Society for Neuroscience|date=August 27, 2013|access-date=June 15, 2015|archive-date=September 12, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170912114143/http://blog.brainfacts.org/2013/08/memento-and-personal-identity/#.VX8Bf_lVhBc|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Author [[Chuck Klosterman]] has written in-depth about ''Memento'' in his essay collection ''[[Sex, Drugs, and Cocoa Puffs: A Low Culture Manifesto]]'', specifically on the diner scene with Leonard and Natalie.<ref>{{cite book |last=Klosterman|first=Chuck|author-link=Chuck Klosterman|date=2003|title=Sex, Drugs, and Cocoa Puffs: A Low Culture Manifesto|url=https://archive.org/details/sexdrugscocoapuf00klos|url-access=registration|publisher=Scribner|isbn=9780743236003}}</ref>

In an interview with Chuck Stephens for ''[[Filmmaker (magazine)|Filmmaker]]'' in 2001, Nolan also stated:

<!--the following should not be in italics, this following is a direct quote and is not italicized in the original source -->{{blockquote|The most interesting part of that for me is that audiences seem very unwilling to believe the stuff that Teddy [Pantoliano] says at the end and yet why? I think it's because people have spent the entire film looking at Leonard's photograph of Teddy, with the caption: "Don't believe his lies." That image really stays in people's heads, and they still prefer to trust that image even after we make it very clear that Leonard's visual recollection is completely questionable. It was quite surprising, and it wasn't planned. What was always planned was that we don't ever step completely outside Leonard's head, and that we keep the audience in that interpretive mode of trying to analyze what they want to believe or not. For me, the crux of the movie is that the one guy who might actually be the authority on the truth of what happened is played by Joe Pantoliano ... who is so untrustworthy, especially given the baggage he carries in from his other movies: he's already seen by audiences as this character actor who's always unreliable. I find it very frightening, really, the level of uncertainty and malevolence Joe brings to the film.<ref>{{Cite web | last=Stephens | first=Chuck | title=Past Imperfect | url=http://www.filmmakermagazine.com/archives/issues/winter2001/features/past_imperfect.php#.V0Rjd4bRY8o | work=Filmmaker | date=Winter 2001 | access-date=December 9, 2016 | archive-date=October 26, 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211026143757/https://www.filmmakermagazine.com/archives/issues/winter2001/features/past_imperfect.php#.V0Rjd4bRY8o | url-status=live }}</ref>}}

===Awards and accolades===
Because Jonathan Nolan's short story was not published before the film was released, it was nominated for Original Screenplay instead of [[Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay|Adapted Screenplay]] and both Christopher and Jonathan received a nomination.
